## Baracoa — a picturesque corner of Cuba

Baracoa is located between two scenic bays in the Cabo Maisí area of the island. Diego Velázquez reached this area in 1512. Baracoa is the oldest European settlement in Cuba.

Nearby are national parks, including Alejandro de Humboldt National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site with extensive forests; El Yunque mountain, whose perfectly flat summit is covered in dense vegetation; preserved Spanish forts; and beautiful beaches.

Bariloche, officially San Carlos de Bariloche, lies on the shore of Lake Nahuel Huapi in the central Patagonian Andes. The city is surrounded by mountain peaks, lakes and forests of Nahuel Huapi National Park.

Downtown Bariloche has cafés, restaurants and shops. It is also home to the Cathedral of Our Lady of Nahuel Huapi, built in 1946 and listed as a National Historic Monument.

Popular nearby sights include Mount Campanario and its viewpoint, Playa Bonita, the Llao Llao Peninsula, Lake Moreno, Huemul Island, St. Edward's Chapel and El Trébol Bay.

In winter, Bariloche is known for skiing. Lifts operate on Mount Catedral, about 2,388 m high, and Mount Otto, about 1,405 m high. Spring and summer bring outdoor excursions, while in autumn the forests around the lakes change color.

Barinas marks the transition from the Venezuelan Andes to the plains of Los Llanos. In the region of the same name, mountain areas border vast lowlands, so the scenery changes noticeably during the journey. This part of Venezuela makes traveling between contrasting landscapes an experience in itself.

Travel itineraries reach Barinas after Andean settlements and roads through cloud forest. The journey then continues toward rural estates and natural areas of the plains. The region connects mountainous Venezuela with Los Llanos and reveals changes in terrain, vegetation and the rural landscape along the way.

Climb to Mirador de la Baronesa for a view over Floreana's northern coast. From a small hill, a turquoise bay fringed by mangroves comes into view. Dark stretches of shoreline and dry vegetation accentuate the color of the water. A short path ends with steeper steps, after which the panoramic view is a welcome place to pause.

The viewpoint is named after a woman who called herself a baroness and lived on Floreana in the 1930s. Her disappearance became part of the island's history. The guide tells stories of settlers and events that inspired books and films; the view itself helps you imagine people waiting for ships to arrive on this remote shore.

The lookout offers a clear view of the bay's shape, which you can compare with its appearance from a boat. If the visit includes a walk along the mangroves, the coastal exploration continues at the water's edge. This spot appeals to travelers who enjoy natural panoramas intertwined with human stories. Stay for a photograph, then look out at the ocean once more without the camera.
